newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl prepares for crisis talks with miners' union.
newsitem.headline: Kohl prepares for crisis talks with miners' union.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl prepared to meet mining union leaders on Thursday for crisis talks aimed at appeasing thousands of angry miners who threatened to besiege Bonn in protest at planned subsidy cuts.

The miners paralysed Bonn's government district for three days but heeded union calls on Wednesday to retreat to nearby Cologne. They said they would return to the city if no satisfactory compromise was reached in the talks.

There were some hints of compromise as Kohl said he saw chances of an agreement and coalition sources said they were considering improving short-term welfare benefits for miners to ease the pain of the cuts.
Kohl had called off the crisis talks at short notice on Tuesday because of the threat of violence, and said he would meet miners' leaders on Thursday (0800 GMT) only if the protests in Bonn stopped.
"If the talks do not go our way we will all be back -- 50,000, 100,000 miners!" IG Bergbau union leader Hans Berger told his members in a hoarse address on Wednesday.
Around 8,000 brawny pit workers from Saar state on the French border, who had held a raucous rally in Bonn on Wednesday, spent the night in a tent village in the grounds of Cologne football stadium.
"If we don't get a reasonable result, we'll be back and all hell will be let loose," said one miner from Saarbruecken.
IG Bergbau laid on hot food and entertainment for the men, many clad in dusty overalls and hard-hats.
Kohl said he believed the talks would succeed "with a bit of goodwill". But he insisted his plan was fair.
Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out last Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the 6.5 billion marks unions have proposed.

Industry sources said mining company Ruhrkohle and utility Veba had put forward a new plan suggesting the government raise its offer by an annual 650 million marks until 2000 to stave off the closure of several mines and job losses.

In a release ahead of publication, the Berliner Morgenpost daily reported that coalition sources said Kohl was ready to increase his offer by 300 million marks per year, although some of that would have to come from state government coffers.

But some commentators said if Kohl backed down on this issue he would lay his government open to pressure from all sides to give up strict budget discipline necessary for qualification for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The danger of an increasingly aggressive wave of demonstrations is completely real," Die Welt daily said in an editorial released ahead of publication on Thursday.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) also made more conciliatory noises, saying for the first time they would not continue boycotting tax reform talks with the government even if Kohl failed to make a satisfactory offer to the pit workers.
But the SPD, which rules the two main mining states, said tempers would flare if there were no concessions on Thursday.
"You must make it clear your nerves are as strong as his (Kohl's)," Franz Muentefering, SPD party manager told miners.
The free-market Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners and the main force behind the plans, hinted they could amend the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.
"We could reorganise them (subsidies) to make the pace of the closures and the transition more bearable," FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told Bonn's General Anzeiger daily.
Miners focused their anger on the FDP by locking the party out of its offices for three days They ended their blockade on Wednesday but left the building ringed with steel chains.
Bonn argues it can no longer afford to pay over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
But IG Bergbau says the plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
